title: Multi-head attention
summary: One head learns one way of looking. Multi-head attention runs h heads side by side, each with its own queries, keys and values of width d/h, concatenates their outputs back to width d, and mixes them with an output projection W_O. In code, one projection is reshaped from (T, d) to (h, T, d/h) so every head is computed in one batched matrix product.
llm_link: Every attention layer in a GPT is multi-head: GPT-2 small, for example, has 12 heads in each of its 12 layers, with d = 768 split into heads of width 64. Interpretability research studies these heads individually, because many of them specialise.
key_ideas: Several heads run in parallel, each with its own W_Q, W_K, W_V and its own attention weights.
Head width d_head = d / h, so the total cost stays close to one wide head.
Head outputs are concatenated back to (T, d) and multiplied by a learned output projection W_O.
Reshape trick: (T, d) → (T, h, d_head) → transpose → (h, T, d_head); scores are (h, T, T).
Attention, with any number of heads, has no idea of token order; that is the next lesson.

quiz.q: d = 512 and h = 8. Predict the shape of the batched score tensor for a sequence of T = 10 tokens.
quiz.explain: Each of the 8 heads has its own (T, T) = (10, 10) score table, stacked along the head axis.

quiz.q: With d = 768 and 12 heads, what is the width of each head's queries and keys?
quiz.explain: d / h = 768 / 12 = 64. This is the configuration of GPT-2 small.

quiz.q: What is the job of the output projection W_O?
options: It mixes the concatenated head outputs so their findings combine into one update per token
It turns token IDs into vectors
quiz.explain: Concatenation just places the head outputs side by side. W_O lets each output dimension draw on every head.

quiz.q: Compared with one head of width d, h heads of width d/h cost…
quiz.explain: The projections have the same total size, and the score tables multiply narrower vectors. The total work stays close to one wide head (there are h small score tables instead of one).

quiz.q: Why might an LLM benefit from many heads per layer?
options: Each head can track a different relationship at once, such as the previous token or a grammatical dependency
More heads make the context window longer
Heads replace the need for training
Each head handles a different language
quiz.explain: A single softmax gives one weighting per token. Several heads give several independent weightings, which trained models use for different jobs.

problems.title: Shape drill: reshape and transpose
problems.prompt:
Multi-head attention is mostly shape bookkeeping. Predict every shape, then print to check.

Rules: reshape keeps the order of the numbers and just regroups them; transpose(1, 0, 2) swaps the first two axes; transpose(0, 2, 1) swaps the last two; @ on two 3D arrays does one matrix product per entry of the first axis.
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

T, d, h = 5, 8, 2
dh = d // h                                  # width of one head
Q = np.zeros((T, d))
Qr = Q.reshape(T, h, dh)                     # cut each row into h slices
Qh = Qr.transpose(1, 0, 2)                   # heads first
Kh = np.zeros((h, T, dh))
Vh = np.zeros((h, T, dh))
S = Qh @ Kh.transpose(0, 2, 1)               # @ on 3D arrays: one matrix product per head
Oh = S @ Vh
merged = Oh.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(T, d)

# Predict each shape as a tuple, e.g. (4, 3), BEFORE printing anything.
# Then check yourself with print(<expression>.shape).
answers = {
    "Qr": None,
    "Qh": None,
    "Kh.transpose(0, 2, 1)": None,
    "S": None,
    "Oh": None,
    "Oh.transpose(1, 0, 2)": None,
    "merged": None,
}

tests.name: shape of Qr
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['Qr']
real = np.shape(Qr)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for Qr'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but Qr has shape {real}. reshape keeps the T rows and cuts each row of d = 8 numbers into h = 2 slices of 4.'

tests.name: shape of Qh
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['Qh']
real = np.shape(Qh)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for Qh'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but Qh has shape {real}. transpose(1, 0, 2) swaps the first two axes, so the heads axis comes first.'

tests.name: shape of Kh.transpose(0, 2, 1)
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['Kh.transpose(0, 2, 1)']
real = np.shape(Kh.transpose(0, 2, 1))
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for Kh.transpose(0, 2, 1)'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but Kh.transpose(0, 2, 1) has shape {real}. This keeps the head axis and swaps the last two, giving one Kᵀ of shape (dh, T) per head.'

tests.name: shape of S
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['S']
real = np.shape(S)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for S'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but S has shape {real}. With 3D arrays, @ multiplies matching pairs along the first axis: (h, T, dh) @ (h, dh, T) gives (h, T, T), one score table per head.'

tests.name: shape of Oh
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['Oh']
real = np.shape(Oh)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for Oh'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but Oh has shape {real}. (h, T, T) @ (h, T, dh) gives (h, T, dh): each head mixes its own values.'

tests.name: shape of Oh.transpose(1, 0, 2)
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['Oh.transpose(1, 0, 2)']
real = np.shape(Oh.transpose(1, 0, 2))
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for Oh.transpose(1, 0, 2)'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but Oh.transpose(1, 0, 2) has shape {real}. Swapping the first two axes back puts tokens first again.'

tests.name: shape of merged
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['merged']
real = np.shape(merged)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for merged'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but merged has shape {real}. reshape(T, d) glues the h slices of each row back together, h × dh = d.'

M=np.arange(40.0).reshape(5,8)
out=split_heads(M,2)
assert out is not None, 'split_heads returned None'
assert out.shape==(2,5,4), f'expected (h, T, dh) = (2, 5, 4), got {out.shape}'

tests.name: head k holds the right columns
tests.code:
import numpy as np
M=np.arange(40.0).reshape(5,8)
out=split_heads(M,2)
assert np.array_equal(out[0],M[:,:4]), 'head 0 should be columns 0-3 of every row'
assert np.array_equal(out[1],M[:,4:]), 'head 1 should be columns 4-7 of every row. If you reshaped straight to (h, T, dh) the numbers are grouped wrongly: reshape to (T, h, dh) first, then transpose.'

tests.name: merge undoes split
tests.code:
import numpy as np
M=np.random.default_rng(1).normal(size=(6,12))
for h in (1,2,3,4,6):
    back=merge_heads(split_heads(M,h))
    assert back is not None, 'merge_heads returned None'
    assert np.array_equal(back,M), f'merge_heads(split_heads(M, {h})) should give M back exactly'

problems.title: Multi-head attention (GPT, step 5)
problems.prompt:
Build multi-head attention the straightforward way, with a loop over heads. The starter has your GPT so far, plus attend(Q, K, V): last lesson's scaled, causal attention working on already-projected matrices.

Write multi_head_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, n_heads): project once, give head k the columns k*dh:(k+1)*dh of Q, K and V, run attend on each, concatenate the results side by side, and multiply by Wo. The output has the same shape as X.

(The tests compare your loop with the batched reshape version from the drill.)
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    e = np.exp(x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def causal_mask(T):
    return np.triu(np.full((T, T), -np.inf), k=1)

def attend(Q, K, V):
    """Scaled, causal attention on already-projected Q, K, V (lesson 9.6)."""
    T, dk = Q.shape
    A = softmax(Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(dk) + causal_mask(T), axis=-1)
    return A @ V

# ---- the character-level GPT so far (lessons 9.1 to 9.6) ----
text = "hello world"
vocab = sorted(set(text))
stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(vocab)}
def encode(s):
    return [stoi[ch] for ch in s]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, n_heads = 8, 2
E = rng.normal(size=(len(vocab), d))
X = E[np.array(encode("hello"))]               # (T, d) = (5, 8)
Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo = (rng.normal(size=(d, d)) / np.sqrt(d) for _ in range(4))

# ---- step 5: multi-head attention (this lesson) ----
def multi_head_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, n_heads):
    """Project once, run each head on its own slice of columns, concatenate, project with Wo. Returns (T, d)."""
    Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv           # each (T, d)
    d = Q.shape[1]
    dh = d // n_heads
    outs = []
    # TODO: for each head k, take columns k*dh:(k+1)*dh of Q, K and V,
    #       run attend(...) on them and append the (T, dh) result to outs
    # TODO: concatenate the head outputs side by side (np.concatenate(outs, axis=1)) -> (T, d)
    # TODO: return that @ Wo

tests.name: shape (T, d)
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out=multi_head_attention(X,Wq,Wk,Wv,Wo,2)
assert out is not None, 'return the projected output'
assert out.shape==(5,8), f'the output should have the same shape as X, (5, 8), got {np.shape(out)}'

tests.name: matches the batched version
tests.code:
import numpy as np
def _ref(X,Wq,Wk,Wv,Wo,h):
    T,d=X.shape;dh=d//h
    sp=lambda M:M.reshape(T,h,dh).transpose(1,0,2)
    Q,K,V=sp(X@Wq),sp(X@Wk),sp(X@Wv)
    S=Q@K.transpose(0,2,1)/np.sqrt(dh)+np.triu(np.full((T,T),-np.inf),k=1)
    e=np.exp(S-S.max(-1,keepdims=True));A=e/e.sum(-1,keepdims=True)
    return (A@V).transpose(1,0,2).reshape(T,d)@Wo
for h in (1,2,4):
    out=multi_head_attention(X,Wq,Wk,Wv,Wo,h)
    assert np.allclose(out,_ref(X,Wq,Wk,Wv,Wo,h)), f'with {h} heads your result differs from the reshape-based reference. Check the column slices, the scaling by sqrt(dh) (inside attend) and the final @ Wo.'

tests.name: one head with Wo = I is plain attention
tests.code:
import numpy as np
I=np.eye(8)
out=multi_head_attention(X,Wq,Wk,Wv,I,1)
assert np.allclose(out,attend(X@Wq,X@Wk,X@Wv)), 'with one head and an identity output projection the result should equal a single attention head'

tests.name: still causal
tests.code:
import numpy as np
a=multi_head_attention(X,Wq,Wk,Wv,Wo,2)
X2=X.copy();X2[-1]+=5
b=multi_head_attention(X2,Wq,Wk,Wv,Wo,2)
assert np.allclose(a[:-1],b[:-1]), 'changing the last token changed earlier outputs: every head must use the causal mask'

hints: cols = slice(k * dh, (k + 1) * dh); Q[:, cols] is head k's queries.
outs.append(attend(Q[:, cols], K[:, cols], V[:, cols]))
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    e = np.exp(x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def causal_mask(T):
    return np.triu(np.full((T, T), -np.inf), k=1)

def attend(Q, K, V):
    """Scaled, causal attention on already-projected Q, K, V (lesson 9.6)."""
    T, dk = Q.shape
    A = softmax(Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(dk) + causal_mask(T), axis=-1)
    return A @ V

# ---- the character-level GPT so far (lessons 9.1 to 9.6) ----
text = "hello world"
vocab = sorted(set(text))
stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(vocab)}
def encode(s):
    return [stoi[ch] for ch in s]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, n_heads = 8, 2
E = rng.normal(size=(len(vocab), d))
X = E[np.array(encode("hello"))]               # (T, d) = (5, 8)
Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo = (rng.normal(size=(d, d)) / np.sqrt(d) for _ in range(4))

# ---- step 5: multi-head attention (this lesson) ----
def multi_head_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, n_heads):
    """Project once, run each head on its own slice of columns, concatenate, project with Wo. Returns (T, d)."""
    Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv           # each (T, d)
    d = Q.shape[1]
    dh = d // n_heads
    outs = []
    for k in range(n_heads):
        cols = slice(k * dh, (k + 1) * dh)
        outs.append(attend(Q[:, cols], K[:, cols], V[:, cols]))
    return np.concatenate(outs, axis=1) @ Wo
